items.item: Vertex reordering is an orthogonal second idea from the representation itself: CSR/CSC can be built over any vertex numbering, and reordering is strictly a pre-processing relabelling step before that construction, not a change to CSR's own two arrays or its two-pass algorithm.

items.item: Degree sort, RCM and community order all pursue the identical goal (put a vertex's own neighbours at numerically nearby labels, so their offsets/targets entries land physically close in memory) by three different signals: raw degree alone, breadth-first visiting order from a low-degree start, and detected cluster membership — not three unrelated techniques.

items.item: The measured cache-locality win is real but conditional, per the degree-sort paper itself: the paper reports its number against a specific baseline and a specific pairing (degree sort plus CSR segmenting together) — this topic's own smaller-scale measurement reports its own real, exact number (an 8.0x cache-line reduction), not the paper's 4x/2x figures as if they transfer unchanged.

A degree-sort reordering can, on a graph with roughly uniform degree, do little for locality since sorting by a near-constant value is close to a random relabelling — the technique's benefit is real but graph-dependent, not universal across every sparse graph.

RCM's own first step (choose a peripheral, i.e. lowest-degree, vertex to start from) matters: starting BFS from an arbitrary vertex instead of a peripheral one changes which vertices end up with nearby labels and can produce a worse bandwidth reduction.

Reordering is a permutation applied once, before construction; it changes which array index a given vertex owns, never the vertex's own identity, out-edges, or any value already computed about the graph — a point easy to blur when the topic's own visuals redraw the "same" vertex at a new position.
